newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Still problems over Hong Kong boat people, UK says.
newsitem.headline: Still problems over Hong Kong boat people, UK says.

text.p: Britain and Vietnam made good progress in talks on Thursday on the repatriation of Vietnamese boat people from Hong Kong but there was still disagreement over some refugees of Chinese origin, a senior British official said.

The official was speaking after British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind met Vietnamese Foreign Minister Nguyen Manh Cam in Singapore to discuss the issue of the boat people, which has dogged relations between the two countries since the 1980s.
Rifkind and Ngyuen were in Singapore for meetings of Asian and European foreign ministers.
More than 110,000 Vietnamese refugees have passed through Hong Kong over the last six years, many arriving in the British colony by sea in tiny boats.
Almost all these refugees have since travelled on to third countries or returned home to Vietnam under the auspices of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.
But Hong Kong authorities say there are approximately 5,500 Vietnamese left in the territory, of which only 2,500 have so far been granted the right to return to Vietnam.
China has said all the refugees must leave Hong Kong before it takes over the territory from Britain on July 1.

Of the remaining group of roughly 3,000 refugees, some 1,000 are stranded because they do not have "household" documents proving they had a home in Vietnam. The rest are ethnic Chinese who were previously residents in Vietnam.
A senior British official said Nguyen had confirmed that the refugees lacking household documents would be allowed to return but there had been little progress on the ethnic Chinese.

"One problem has been people who, though clearly accepted as Vietnamese, have not had their household registration (documents). We have noted an agreement by the Vietnamese authorities to receive those people," the official told reporters.
"There are still outstanding problems on the issue of ethnic Chinese, what the Vietnamese term non-nationals. On that there will continue to be discussions," he said.
Before entering the meeting, Rifkind told a news conference he was hopeful all the refugees could be repatriated before the handover of Hong Kong to China.
"We believe it is practical to have the process complete before June 30," Rifkind said.
The British official said this remained Hong Kong's aim.

"We have already made substantial progress and there is going to be continued progress over the months ahead. Our objective remains, and it is a realistic objective, to clear that backlog by June 30," he said.
"The process is not really behind schedule. It is technically perfectly possible to return this number of people in that time," he said.
Leaving the meeting, Nguyen confirmed to reporters that there had been no agreement on the ethnic Chinese refugees.
"According to Vietnamese law we cannot accept non-nationality people," Nguyen said.
